The 1912 Summer Olympics. Held in Stockholm, Sweden, the 1912 Summer Olympics marked a dramatic expansion of the Games' scale. Nearly twenty-four hundred athletes from twenty-eight nations participated—nearly ten times the size of the 1896 Games held sixteen years earlier. The program had grown to include one hundred and two events across fourteen different sports, establishing a new standard for Olympic scope.

The most dominant figure of these Games was Jim Thorpe, a Native American athlete who displayed exceptional versatility and strength. Thorpe won gold medals in both the pentathlon and the decathlon, demonstrating mastery across a wide range of athletic disciplines. His achievement seemed to epitomize Olympic excellence.

Yet Thorpe's story took a darker turn. In 1913, just a year after his triumph, his medals were rescinded when it was revealed he had played semi-professional baseball before the Games—then a violation of the strict amateur status rules that governed Olympic eligibility. This scandal marked a turning point in Olympic politics around the definition and enforcement of amateurism. Though his medals were taken away, they were finally restored to Thorpe posthumously in 1983.

The 1912 Olympics also saw progress toward inclusion. For the first time, women were permitted to compete in the Games, though opportunities remained severely limited—they could only compete in swimming and diving, while track and field remained male-only for many decades to come. Sweden hosted the Games efficiently and smoothly, establishing Stockholm as a well-organized Olympic city.
